reason: Collisions among the orbiting debris are a plausible first step toward gathering the Moon or sending material back inward.
expectation: Collisions will change the debris into a more concentrated or sorted population.

alternatives.reason: Material beyond the disruption region may be able to gather into the Moon.

effect: Collisions redistributed the debris into a spreading ring, which may now separate into inward- and outward-moving material.
reaction: The distinction between a spreading disk and a solid ring is useful.
reason: Material spreading beyond the tidal disruption region should be able to gather into a Moon.
expectation: The outer material will become available to clump together.

alternatives.reason: I could check its available paths if the expected outward route is not compatible.

effect: The outer ring has produced growing moonlets that can survive tidal disruption and merge.
reaction: It is satisfying to see why their location matters.
reason: Gravity within a dense swarm should help the moonlets merge into a larger body.
expectation: The moonlets will gather into a young Moon.

effect: The moonlets have gathered into a hot young Moon; it still needs to cool and form a crust.
reaction: The Moon coming together is satisfying, though its early history remains uncertain.
reason: Radiation escaping into space should cool the young Moon and help its crust form.
expectation: The Moon will cool enough to develop a crust.

effect: Cooling produced lunar magma-ocean crystals, but the crust has not yet formed.
reaction: The distinction between crystallization and crust formation is useful.
reason: Gravity can separate minerals by density, potentially allowing lighter crystals to form a crust.

choice.combine: Crystals in the lunar magma ocean

expectation: The crystals will separate, with lighter minerals contributing to a lunar crust.

effect: The crystals combined with the young Moon to form a buoyant feldspar-rich layer; gravity was not the compatible partner.
reaction: The compatibility feedback clarified that the crust forms within the Moon.
reason: The floating layer likely needs to lose heat to become a cooling crust.
expectation: The layer will cool into a lunar crust.

alternatives.reason: I could check its compatible partners if cooling is not the next step.

effect: The Moon now has a pale early crust; returning inward-falling debris to Earth remains.
reaction: The distinction between the early crust and the later dark maria is useful.
reason: The spreading ring may supply debris that Earth's gravity pulls back inward.
expectation: Some ring material will fall back toward Earth.

alternatives.reason: The surviving Earth may be the direct partner for returning debris.

effect: Earth's gravity sent part of the spreading ring back toward the planet; the falling rock still needs to reach Earth.
reaction: The split between Moon-forming and returning debris is clear.
reason: The falling rock should return to the surviving Earth.
expectation: The debris will rejoin Earth, completing the remaining goal.

effect: The falling debris rejoined and reheated Earth, completing the remaining goal while leaving some of its volatile inventory intact.
reaction: The returning material made a satisfying counterpart to the Moon-forming branch.

mostWorthwhile.text: Sending the spreading ring beyond the tidal disruption region was most worthwhile: it connected the Moon’s growth to where self-gravitating clumps can survive.

leastWorthwhile.text: The final return to Earth was a fairly predictable completion step, though it clarified that reaccretion also adds heat.

surprise.text: Cooling first produced crystals rather than a finished crust; buoyant feldspar then helped form the outer layer.

arbitrary.text: Using the crystals with the young Moon rather than gravity was not obvious to me, although the feedback explained that the layer forms within the Moon.

continue.text: Yes. I would choose to continue because the branching paths and concise physical explanations made me curious about how the remade Earth develops.
